paragraphs: A fine rain was falling when the gates of Jiankang opened. Doors along the imperial avenue stayed shut. Only a few charcoal sellers huddled under the eaves with their carrying poles. By the time Fu Jian’s carriage reached Vermilion Bird Gate, the ceremonial officers had formed the musicians, canopies, banners, and ranks for receiving the surrender. Scarlet standards vanished into the wet mist. In other years, when an army entered the capital, the people had been driven out to kneel along the streets. Today no one waited. Even the children had been carried back into the courtyards.

Fu Jian dismounted outside the gate and ordered the musicians dismissed. Only three hundred guards were to accompany him. Fu Rong climbed down from the following carriage, leaning on his staff. His right leg had been crushed beneath a fallen horse at the Fei River; in damp weather he always had to pause before taking his first step. The brothers entered side by side, moving slowly. An old Beifu soldier on gate duty had not changed his uniform. He showed no expression at the sight of Qin’s approaching banners, but handed over the gate keys and entry-and-exit register for examination by officers from both sides, as the new treaty required.

A Jin banner that had flown over the gate for many years had been taken down. The flagpole stood bare, rainwater dripping down its ropes onto the stone wall. Fu Jian glanced up without asking why a Qin banner had not immediately gone up in its place. The general assigned to take over the gate understood that Jingkou’s former soldiers had first to be mustered and relieved, and uncounted weapons still lay locked in the arsenal. If anyone hurried to plant a flag, the newly opened city might close its gates once more.

At a corner of the imperial avenue, two surrendered soldiers were sweeping loose stones from the road. A Qin officer thought them too slow and raised his whip. Before the lash could strike, Fu Rong caught the whip.
“Soldiers who have laid down their swords must either be registered and judged or sent home with land to farm. Do you take them for packhorses?”

Recognizing the Prince of Yangping, the officer dropped to his knees. Fu Rong let go. The whip fell on the wet stones and splashed up dirty water. Fu Jian made no speech about the incident. He ordered the military magistrate to record it and examine the authority under which the men had been assigned the labor. If they had been properly hired, they were still to be paid the posted wage. The surrendered men picked up their brooms and went on sweeping. After the carriage passed, one glanced up and looked again at the discarded whip before returning to his work.

The procession had been due to proceed directly to the imperial compound. But Fu Jian changed course in the street and went first to the Jin ancestral temple. A scholar-official traveling with the court hurried forward in alarm. It was against ritual, he said, for a sovereign to enter the ancestral temple of a fallen state; the people of Jiangnan might even mistake the visit for fear of the Sima family’s legitimate claim. Fu Jian asked whether the temple had been inspected for weapons and fire hazards. The scholar was taken aback. The guards remained at their posts, he said, and the temple keeper refused to hand over the key.
“Then we shall ask the keeper first.”

Moss had grown on the eaves of the old ancestral temple. Gu Wei, who had guarded it for forty-two years, sat on the threshold holding its keys, his ceremonial cap and robes unchanged. Beside him was a bamboo chest of ritual vessels. When told the Qin ruler had come, he rose and tried to keep his back straight.
“This temple houses the ancestors of the Sima family,” the old man said. “If the Qin ruler has come to tear it down, tear down this old servant first.”
Fu Jian saw the dates of repairs carved into the lid of the bamboo chest. The last had been done only the previous month; the wood still showed pale and fresh.
“I have come to announce before them that the fighting has ceased.”
Gu Wei shook his head stubbornly. “Only Jin’s descendants may offer sacrifice to Jin’s ancestors. It is against the rites for the Qin ruler to do so.”
“Then lead the way. I will bow once in the outer courtyard.”

The old keeper said nothing, but finally unlocked the gate. The hinges had not been replaced for years and turned with a harsh rasp. There were no musicians inside. Moss grew between the stone steps; the curtains of the main hall hung low, and the last faint fragrance of lamp oil lingered. Fu Jian bowed in the outer courtyard. He did not enter the space of the ancestral tablets or order any inscription changed. Gu Wei remained standing beside him and did not call himself a subject afterward.

On the return journey, Fu Rong said the old man would give the censors in Guanzhong a long list of offenses against imperial dignity. Fu Jian replied that the treaty allowed Gu Wei to guard the temple. If the court wanted to replace him, it must first determine whether he had privately armed retainers or damaged ritual vessels; he could not be punished merely for refusing to kneel. Fu Rong looked at him for a while and laughed. “Imperial brother, now you mean to put even a man’s right to dislike you into the statutes.”
“He has kept that temple for forty-two years,” Fu Jian said. “I have been here only half a day.”

The next day Fu Jian went to inspect the military rolls at the old Beifu camp north of the city. Liu Yu stood beneath the gate, wearing black armor washed and worn over many years; its patches were stitched unevenly. Several Qin generals disapproved. Fu Rong, however, first asked when the old soldiers would receive their first payment of arrears.

Liu Yu reported that the money and cloth released by the court had arrived, but the grain in Jin’s former stores was still being audited. The lists of dead, missing, and disabled soldiers from the various camps had not yet been reconciled, and that had to come first. Fu Jian ordered the grain officers from both armies to open the chests in public and make the first payments according to the conversion schedule. While Guanzhong coin and Jiangnan’s old coin circulated together, any official who used currency exchange to withhold so much as one coin would be questioned first by military justice.

The camp was packed with former soldiers awaiting their payments. They did not cheer. An old company commander asked loudly whether Beifu soldiers who had once killed Qin men were to be counted as criminals. Fu Jian replied that casualties inflicted in battle by men serving their respective lords were not private crimes. Killing prisoners, burning civilian homes, or pillaging property would be investigated according to the evidence from each incident, and the same rule applied to Qin troops. The old commander asked how compensation could be paid when a dead man’s family could not be found. Fu Rong pointed to the family-tracing register compiled from both armies' rolls. He told the man to report the name; the public granary would hold the payment in trust until the relatives were located.

Looking at that register, Liu Yu remembered military families in Jingkou circling the camp gates for years with old slips promising arrears. For the men already dead, this grain and money came painfully late. Yet if their claims were canceled today, no one would ever acknowledge what had been owed to them before. He told a military clerk to check once more the name of Madam Wu’s elder son. She had not come to the parade ground; she was arranging the funeral of her younger boy. A neighbor brought an old receipt on her behalf, its torn corner stitched with thread.

It was the receipt for the first installment of arrears she had recovered for her elder son. A short length of old hemp had been sewn into its folded corner. The clerk asked the neighbor to tell her the remaining grain would be paid in three more installments. Madam Wu sent back only one message: make the seal impression clear, and do not write her surname Wu with the wrong character again. At home she had an old wooden chest containing the straw sandals of both sons. She would no longer allow others to get their names wrong.

Behind the barracks, a roof tile suddenly came flying and grazed Fu Jian’s forehead. His guards drew their swords and searched the area, dragging a boy of ten or so from the foot of a wall. Mud covered his clothes. He clamped his mouth shut and would not beg for mercy even when held to the ground. Liu Yu recognized him as the son of a soldier killed from the Eastern Headquarters' Left Camp. His home had burned during the mutiny, and he was living temporarily beside the barracks.
“Why did you throw the tile?” Fu Jian asked.
The boy stared at him. “My father died at the Fei River. Your people killed him.”

The expressions of the Qin soldiers around them darkened. Fu Jian’s guards asked to drag the boy away. Liu Yu, too, knew that an assault upon the Heavenly King in front of an army could not simply be dismissed under the law. Fu Jian ordered a clerk first to check whether the boy’s father was indeed on the military roll and whether his compensation remained unpaid. He then asked them to find a guarantor who would take the child in. Officials were to review the offense according to the injury caused and the alarm to the imperial entourage. The guards were not to break his bones in private.
Seeing the blood at Fu Jian’s temple, fear flashed in the boy’s eyes, but his words remained defiant. “Does complaining to the officials do any good?”
“You must bring them facts,” Fu Jian said. “Someone must also ask on your behalf about your father’s military merit and the pay owed him.”
“And if the officials won’t listen?”
Fu Jian looked toward Liu Yu. “General Liu, tell him where he can take his complaint.”

Liu Yu named the Jingkou military office, the household bureau of the southern capital, and the Secretariat’s review office. The boy was bewildered by much of it, but understood the last sentence: a clerk could write his petition for him free of charge. When he was escorted out of the camp he still had not saluted the Qin banner, but he held a family-tracing certificate endorsed by the military office tightly in his fist.

Fu Rong afterward told his brother that people in Guanzhong would certainly ask why, after being struck by a tile, he had allowed a southern boy who dared point at the Heavenly King and declare his hatred to remain free. Pressing a cloth against his wound, Fu Jian said, “If all he does next time is curse me, let the provincial and county offices deal with what belongs to them. If everything depends on my personally showing mercy once, then all the court’s work has been for nothing.”
Jiankang’s first month was far from peaceful.

A small flotilla from Shanyang waited at a ferry for two whole days. A boy aboard who had only just learned to write his own name held both a Qin household registration and an old Jin deed of residence. He asked the checkpoint officer on which bank he would henceforth owe his grain tax. The officer had never seen that pair of documents before. He took the boy under a shelter, then asked clerks from both sides to examine the papers together. At dusk the boy still had no answer. Leaning against the boat, he wrote his name three times on the wet planks. As he completed the last, the traces of water were already spreading apart.

Grain brought across from Qin’s northern bank had to pass through two river mouths, and a shipment of damp millet spoiled. Several great Jiangnan families had boxes of land deeds carried to the southern capital’s Secretariat, afraid their holdings might be confiscated overnight as rebel property. Northern soldiers rewarded for their service asked whether twenty years of war could end with nothing for them but the old fields they had held in Guanzhong, while the rich land of Wu Commandery remained in the hands of those who had defended the city against them. A veteran general petitioned for Jiangnan estates to be granted to meritorious military households. The argument at court went on until mud stained everyone’s robes and shoes.

Fu Jian had the fourteen-article treaty from the Fei River brought out and spread upon his desk. Its promise of no sudden change to the land system for three years, and of examination of existing offices and property case by case, had been sealed only yesterday. The old general argued that treaties must not shelter rebels and that men who died for Qin deserved compensation. Fu Jian ordered military headquarters first to list the army’s dead and disabled and its unpaid wages, then determine what the treasury could actually provide. Those who wished to settle in Jiangnan could be assigned public wasteland or property lawfully confiscated after proven treason; seizing civilian fields was not a military reward.
“Does Your Majesty expect the soldiers to return empty-handed?” the old general asked.

Fu Rong answered, “How much military land have you already received in Hedong? How many installments of your son’s old stipend have you collected? If the accounts are false, audit them too. If they are true, lay out everything still owed and unpaid.”

The general stood seething, but at last fell silent. He was not necessarily persuaded. After the audience he went to several other veterans to discuss submitting a joint memorial. A single day had not taught those men how to govern under new land laws.

On Liu Yu’s third day after receiving the seal of the Jiangnan provisional governor-general, two counties brought competing lawsuits over the same water-powered mill. One cited an old Jin regulation, the other a newly issued Qin waterworks directive. A regional official said the case should for now be judged under the old law; a Qin inspector suspected that the new administration was being rendered powerless. Liu Yu immediately returned one appointment document for reconsideration, attaching the numbers of flood-damaged fields in three villages. He asked Chang’an to review the matter. The inspector, furious, threatened to impeach him for deliberate obstruction. At Liu Yu’s side, Liu Muzhi registered the dates and signatures from both parties one by one and murmured that, when these disputes were reopened three years later, there would probably be no fewer boxes than there were today.

The people of the south did not all yield their allegiance at once either. Some brought their children to the household bureau to reclaim northern guest registrations. Others feared that old debts would be revived if they went home, and could not bear to abandon the thin fields they had finally obtained north of the Huai. Shen Lingyi came south from the northern bank carrying the ashes of her late husband, Zhou Shu. She spent a night in Wuxing and buried his urn in the ancestral cemetery of the Zhou family. The parasol tree still stood at their old house in the village, but strangers lived beneath it. The former owner was willing to let her return and offered substitute tenant land. Shen Lingyi asked only to be allowed to visit the grave, making no claim to the house.
“You have a home on both sides now,” an old woman told her as they parted.

Shen Lingyi shook her head and pointed to a chest of books on the boat. “Of the seventeen pupils who crossed the river with me, some have families now, and some have gone to work in prefectures and counties. Chen Man teaches the younger children in my place, but the school has taken in many newcomers. If I stay away too long, they may lose their lessons again.”

She pressed a leaf from the tree of her old home into a book, then obtained a new river-crossing pass certified by the offices of both north and south. As she traveled north, two merchants at the ferry argued over the meaning of “returning home.” One said that, having regained southern registration, the woman should no longer receive guest farmland in the north. The other said that officials had always written the registers, but a person’s feet decided where that person lived. She did not join their dispute. Sitting at the stern, she opened the exercises her pupils had left at the school, one page after another.

Gu Asheng was at the ferry that day as well. He had left the medical shelter on the northern bank and was carrying hemp cloth for boatmen heading south, hoping to earn the fare for the last leg of his journey. After years of searching for his mother’s grave, he had at last received a letter from an old soldier who had once worked at the county prison. His mother had probably been buried near the salt embankment outside Shangyu, but nobody remembered which mound was hers. He still kept close to his body copies of the old debts from the saltworks. He wanted to return and search with his own eyes.

He told a healer who asked after him that he might never find the grave, and even if he did, he might not know where to kneel. The healer urged him to wait until the south was more settled. But Gu Asheng poured a small pinch of old, hardened salt onto a piece of paper and wrapped it tight. “My mother has waited long enough.” Before the boat sailed, he worked another half day at the ferry and tucked every coin he earned inside his robe.

The possession of Jin’s imperial seal did not relieve the new court of the need to collect grain taxes, correct the errors of former officials, or investigate the private seizure of fields by soldiers. Files piled quickly higher than a man’s shoulder in the Jiangnan administration. Fu Rong, still not fully recovered from his illness, suffered leg pain whenever the weather turned damp, yet often rode out to inspect the integration of the armies.

During one exercise, northern cavalrymen mocked southern sailors for their poor riding; the sailors retorted that the cavalrymen grew so seasick on the Yangtze they could not even lift their swords. Shoving turned into fists on both sides. When Fu Rong arrived he did not ask where the men had been born. He looked at the injured first, established who struck whom, then sentenced them under military discipline to work on the embankments. Those who started the fighting received ten extra days; those who joined in received ten fewer. Medical costs for the injured would be deducted from the offenders' pay.

The old generals grumbled that, now all under heaven had been settled, sending soldiers to dig earth for punishment spoiled the triumph. Leaning against the carriage cushion, Fu Rong looked at the quarrelsome men. “In the old days, when trouble began, we first asked what people a man belonged to and what camp would come to avenge him. Now we first ask which hand he used to strike. Whether they can stay in the same unit depends on whether tomorrow they can eat from the same pot.”

When Fu Pi led part of the old army north, he left his father a secret memorial. The great families of the Three Wu districts were unwilling to surrender complete household registers, the old Beifu troops still remembered the Xie family, and Liu Yu’s standing among the people of Jiangnan was growing. Every word was true. From Chang’an, Fu Hong reported that the treasury was under strain. The clerks and granary funds needed for three years of new registrations faced a considerable shortfall, and several dangerous weirs along the grain-transport route from Luoyang to Huaibei needed repairs first.

Fu Jian placed the two memorials beside each other. He ordered the regional administration and the Secretariat to deal with each matter in turn, and forbade them to postpone repairs to the old garrison-farming canals of the north for the sake of celebrating victory. The jade seal lay in its new case. The army and government now had more work before them than ever.

In Hedong, Liang Cheng had grown too old to pull a cart for long. During the withdrawal from the Fei River years before, he had returned home on a labor-service certificate bearing his name incorrectly. Since then the canals had been built and ruined and repaired, and his family’s wooden waterwheel had had its spokes replaced three times. When a county clerk came to tell him he would have to perform more labor that winter, Liang Cheng asked his son to take the old certificate and make inquiries. He crouched beside the canal listening to the water. His son could read every character on the paper, but first asked whether they would again have to contribute extra labor in place of another village. Liang Cheng said they should find out before deciding; one family could not use an old slip to escape work rightly owed by someone else.

Late in autumn the ministers asked for a new era name. The ceremonial officers proposed names such as “Eternal Unity” and “Establishing the Pole,” with eulogies declaring that all four seas had returned their hearts to the throne and warfare had ended in every quarter. Some urged Fu Jian to perform the great sacrificial rites on Mount Tai. Fu Jian looked up from the grain-transport accounts, listened while the officers read an entire scroll of praise, and asked whether the fugitive households in the Three Wu districts had been registered again and whether several Yangtze ferries were still charging merchants taxes twice. No one could produce a complete answer.

The era name could change; the Mount Tai ceremony would wait. He chose Taihe, “Great Harmony.” Fu Jian deleted the most extravagant praise from the draft decree and added a requirement for three years of institutional review and the public release of accounts each year. A remonstrating officer asked why an edict announcing unification should admit there were matters still unsettled. Fu Jian offered no rebuttal. He set three stacks of unresolved cases on the table: military households in Guanzhong, migrant registers along the Huai, and land deeds in Jiangnan. He left them for the officer to inspect.

Before news of the new era name had reached every district, Jiankang saw its first anti-Qin assassination attempt. A former Jin military clerk attacked a Qin-registered official responsible for collecting grain at night. The official was wounded; the attacker was caught. Several northern generals demanded that the assassin be executed and quartered in the marketplace to awe the public. Former Jiangnan officials petitioned for mercy, saying he had acted out of loyalty to his lost country.

The case established that he had attacked with a weapon out of private anger. It also revealed that the wounded official had illegally collected additional boat taxes. The military justice office judged the offenses separately: the attacker received the lawful penalty, while the official had to repay the taxes and lost his post. People on both sides were dissatisfied. For more than ten days the Jiankang markets were full of argument and occasional shouted abuse. But nobody was dragged into prison merely for speaking a few words in praise of the old dynasty.

Before winter Fu Jian decided to return north. At first the officials of Jiangnan did not believe it. Several men who hoped the emperor would personally rule on their land cases hurried to send mounted messengers begging him to stay. Liu Yu also came to the temporary palace to ask why the Heavenly King was leaving so quickly, now that Jiangnan had only just been settled.

“The autumn grain in Guanzhong must be audited too,” Fu Jian replied. “Every extra day I sit in Jiankang is another day the north imagines all its business must yield to the south. The crown prince has held Chang’an together for years. I cannot leave him forever clearing away what follows me.”
“If you leave this place to me, aren’t you afraid I won’t be able to hold it?”
“I am.”
The answer came so readily that Liu Yu found he could not smile.

Fu Jian took out a copy of the provisional agreement and pointed out the clauses on joint signatures for troop movements, the right to return an appointment once for reconsideration, and the three-year limit. In an urgent military crisis Liu Yu could act first and supply his reasons within ten days. If a Qin inspector obstructed disaster relief, the same documents allowed his impeachment. Liu Yu asked how he could wait for a decree to travel the many days to Chang’an when disaster in Jiangnan could occur in a single night.

“Do what must be done,” Fu Jian said. “Then write clearly why you did it, who died, and how much grain you spent. You required others to account for themselves like that when you were in Jingkou. Now it is your turn.”

Liu Yu studied the agreement for a long time. He had been defeated at the Fei River, and at the walls of Jiankang he had once imagined taking the imperial seal into his own hands. Now all he held was the seal of a three-year regional administration. Qin troops still occupied positions north of the river, and many of the men who had once served beside him would not meet his eyes. Fu Jian did not tell him to be ashamed of his old enmities. Nor did Liu Yu promise the Heavenly King that his allegiance would never again be troubled by doubt. As they parted, he said only, “I will keep these three years. Afterward, as the agreement provides, we shall negotiate again.”
“Good.”

There was no music of triumph when Fu Jian’s procession left Jiankang. Gu Wei, the Jin ancestral temple’s keeper, stood in his old-fashioned blue robes outside the gate and bowed once from afar. A woman selling scallions complained that the guards were blocking the morning market and carried her baskets around the procession. At the entrance to the Beifu barracks, old soldiers saluted Liu Yu; others kept their heads down and went on with their work. Fu Jian noticed it all and ordered no record made of anyone’s discourtesy.
Outside Vermilion Bird Gate, Liu Yu came to see him off. He had more to say, but in the end asked only, “And if it still doesn’t work after three years?”

Fu Jian looked back at the battlements. The new Qin banner hung heavy with rain. Beneath the flagpole lay the same stone steps where guards had stood defending the Jin gate, and the gouge left by an old spear was still visible in the stone.
“Then we shall negotiate again.”
“Some people cannot wait that long.”
“Look after those who cannot wait.”
Fu Rong leaned out of the carriage and saw the two still talking. “If you go on another quarter of an hour, we won’t reach the first relay river before nightfall.”

Fu Jian and Liu Yu exchanged long bows. Liu Yu stood beside the gate for a while, watching the column move north, but did not order drums beaten from the towers as he once would have done in pursuit of an enemy. It occurred to him that one day he too would go far away, while those who remained in Jiangnan would still have to pay taxes, work their fields, and bring lawsuits in these commanderies and counties. What they remembered of him then might be some small matter he had never thought to notice.

On the journey north, new reeds had sprung up around the old army camps by the Fei. Fu Rong’s leg hurt whenever the wind turned cold. He would not allow attendants to fuss over him at the relay stations, yet often sat crookedly once he mounted a horse. When Fu Jian saw how pale he was, he ordered the procession to camp for the night on the old bank of the Fei. The brothers walked down a low slope toward the river, their guards following at a distance. Farmers had long since pulled several old camp stakes from the waterside to use as firewood. Half a broken arrowhead remained buried in the mud.
“That was where your horse fell, down by those shallows,” Fu Jian said, pointing downstream.
Fu Rong looked. “If you truly want to know the spot, you’ll have to bring Liang Hu and the others here. My face was in the mud that day. How could I tell whether the river lay east or west?”

He laughed, then fell silent. In that battle an arrow had struck his mount, and his right leg was pinned beneath the stirrup as it fell. Liang Hu, a veteran of the former Xianbei units, had blocked the gap with his shield; Manu of the Qiang had cut the harness; Zhai Hei and two Di soldiers had lifted the horse clear; Zhao An, a Han crossbowman, had kept his men guarding the banner. The flag had not fallen. Nor had the Qin formation broken ranks to save an imperial brother. Later, when the military clerks verified their merit, the men received rewards on the same camp roll, without being divided again according to their former peoples.
“Twenty years ago, who would have thought they would choose to save me?” Fu Rong said.
“If any one of them fell today,” Fu Jian answered, “the others ought to save him too.”
“They still quarrel often.”
“At least they must live to quarrel again tomorrow.”

In the distance a unit of the new army was making camp. Northern horsemen and southern sailors were fighting over a patch of high ground where they wanted to dry their armor. Two men cursed fiercely in their different accents. A squad leader arrived, divided the ground, and ordered them both to carry water; neither was permitted to draw a knife in private. They went on grumbling as they worked. Only when the bronze ladle struck the cooking pot to announce supper did their curses grow a little shorter.

Watching them, Fu Rong suddenly asked about Murong Chui’s former men. The old general was buried beside the Taihang post road, his gravestone bearing nothing but his name, according to his wishes. Maps, grain vouchers, and march registers from the former Yan camps had been transferred to central military headquarters under their established unit numbers. His death had not brought back their old Yan designations. Fu Rong said there were still men who came to his grave each year, and others who told tales of the old Yan palace more glowingly than they ever had while he was alive.
“Let them pay their respects,” Fu Jian said. “The maps he left behind are more useful than ten additional titles cut into his gravestone.”

He remembered Wang Meng’s warning during his final illness: the court was not yet secure, and a southern expedition would draw out every old grievance across the realm. Back then Fu Jian’s heart had been set on seeing the rivers and mountains united. He had promised not to attack Jin for ten years out of reverence for his old minister, even while secretly counting the years that remained. Now that decade was long past, and Jin’s imperial title had indeed vanished. Yet the temples of ministers who had served the fallen state, the old banners of Liu Yu’s soldiers, and the children Shen Lingyi had taught still had histories of their own.

Fu Jian took the old sheet of paper from inside his robe. It had grown thin from folding, but the five characters of Wang Meng’s pledge, “Do not attack Jin for ten years,” were still clear. Fu Rong examined it for a long time, then sighed. “In the end, brother, you did take Jin.”
“Yes.”
“Are you afraid Jinglüe will curse you from the underworld?”
“If he were still alive, he would first audit how much grain my campaign cost and then ask how many people died.”
“And after that?”
Fu Jian looked across the river. “He would ask whether the people who crossed rivers, mountains, and passes with us in those days can now make a living from their fields.”
Fu Rong gave back the paper and laughed. “That does sound like something Wang Jinglüe would ask.”

Lamps appeared in a village downstream from the relay crossing. A woman stood at the courtyard gate calling her child home. Her voice carried twice across the water with no answer. The third time, there was urgency in her throat. Beside the bank, the drivers of several military carts had already unharnessed their oxen. They were helping relay-station workers carry broken wooden stakes to the roadside so wagon wheels would not sink there the following day. In the dark it was impossible to tell whether they had once been Qin soldiers, Jin soldiers, or laborers in some family’s employ.

Fu Jian watched for a long time, then folded the old paper and returned it to its case. Fu Rong asked whether they could follow the planned road to the next stop tomorrow. Fu Jian nodded. As he mounted, he braced a hand on the saddle and realized his arms were no longer as strong as they had been.

The woman called again. At last a child answered from the distance, the voice thin and bright. Fu Jian turned to watch the river flowing east along the low bank, curling around the old camp stakes. By the bridge a newly posted sentry was learning the password from a man in his squad. He repeated it several times, still with the accent of his home district. His squad leader grew impatient, taught him again, and then handed him the shift-change token.

Chang’an was still a thousand li away. Canals, passes, and homes lay along the night road; tomorrow the government registers would bear fresh disputes. Fu Jian ordered no monument raised on this old riverbank. The relay men lit the lamps for the journey, and the carriages moved slowly north through the valley.
The Fei River flows east, unending, unending.
